python_igraph.notes: Rust port runs the karate fixture in ~81% of python-igraph's median wall time; on ring-of-cliques 4x5 the Rust port is ~3.3x faster (10.3 us vs 33.7 us); on two-K5-bridge the Rust port is ~4.8x faster (4.7 us vs 22.7 us). All three implementations land the same best-Q values.

notes: Hot loop is the greedy merge: pop highest dq from a global BinaryHeap, recompute dq for every shared neighbour (Triangle / Chain-1 / Chain-2 update rules), push updated entries. BTreeMap-per-community keeps mirror updates O(log V) per neighbour.

We use a lazy-deletion strategy on the global heap: stale entries are filtered on pop by validating both endpoints are still alive and that neis[c1][c2] == stored_dq. This avoids the cross-pointer indexed max-heap of the C reference and stays in safe Rust.

Memory layout: Vec<BTreeMap<u32, f64>> for per-community neighbours (O(V + Σ deg)), Vec<bool> for alive, Vec<u32> for cluster ids, Vec<f64> for a[c], plus one BinaryHeap<HeapEntry> shared across all merges.

Asymptotic: with the lazy heap approach the worst case is O(E log² V) (E pushes + O(log V) BTreeMap mirror + O(log V) heap), one factor of log V worse than the Wakita-Tsurumi indexed heap; at Phase-1 graph scales the constant factor is well below python-igraph's Python overhead so net throughput is on par or faster.
